scenario: TechGuard Ltd is a cybersecurity company that provides penetration testing services. Ethical hackers at TechGuard probe clients' IT systems to find weaknesses, but only with written permission.

(AO2) Thorough analysis — critically evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of the legislation with reference to the scenario and wider context. (AO3a) Reaches a well-reasoned and justified conclusion about the overall effectiveness of the CMA, acknowledging its strengths while identifying areas for improvement. (AO3b)

topic: F2.1.5 Data protection legislation — enforcement and penalties
scenario:
DataVault is a major UK credit reference agency that holds personal financial data on over 30 million UK adults. A data breach exposes the credit histories, addresses, and financial details of 8 million people. Investigation reveals that DataVault had: (1) used outdated software with known vulnerabilities; (2) failed to conduct regular security testing; (3) failed to notify the ICO within 72 hours; (4) not appointed a Data Protection Officer (DPO) despite being required to do so.

You should consider:
• DataVault's obligations under UK GDPR
• The consequences of each specific failure
• The effectiveness of UK GDPR as a regulatory framework
• The impact on individuals affected by the breach
question: Evaluate the extent to which DataVault has fulfilled its obligations under UK GDPR and the impact of its failures on individuals, the organisation, and the effectiveness of data protection regulation in the UK.

indicative_content: DataVault as a data controller has extensive obligations under UK GDPR
Obligation to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures (Article 32) — breached by use of outdated software
Known vulnerabilities not patched — this is negligent and clearly falls below the required standard
Failure to conduct regular security testing — further evidence of inadequate security measures
Mandatory 72-hour breach notification to the ICO (Article 33) — failing this is a separate breach
Affected individuals should have been notified where risk to their rights is high (Article 34)
Credit reference agencies processing large volumes of financial data are almost certainly required to appoint a DPO
Failure to appoint a DPO is a serious structural failure under Article 37
The ICO can issue fines of up to £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher)
The scale of the breach (8 million people) and the four separate failings would likely attract a very substantial fine
Individuals whose data was exposed face real financial harm — risk of identity theft, fraud, credit damage
8 million individuals have the right to compensation if they can demonstrate loss or distress
Reputational damage to DataVault could be existential — loss of client confidence in a credit reference agency
The incident demonstrates the need for proactive security rather than reactive patching
UK GDPR's effectiveness: the penalty regime provides strong financial incentives for compliance
However, if enforcement is delayed or fines are insufficient relative to business revenue, deterrence is weakened
The ICO's ability to investigate and enforce in a timely manner is crucial to regulatory effectiveness
The case illustrates that technical, organisational, and procedural failures often combine to create major breaches
A comprehensive data protection framework requires not just legislation but effective enforcement and organisational culture
Conclusion should assess the overall performance of DataVault and the effectiveness of the regulatory regime

level_descriptors.descriptor: No rewardable material.

Demonstrates basic application — identifies one or two GDPR obligations or consequences without developing them in the context of DataVault. (AO2) Demonstrates basic analysis — identifies some implications without exploring how they interrelate. (AO3a) No evaluative conclusion. (AO3b)

Demonstrates good application — discusses several of DataVault's specific failures with reference to relevant UK GDPR articles. Considers impact on individuals and the organisation. (AO2) Demonstrates good analysis — analyses how the failures interact and considers the range of consequences including fines, compensation, and reputational damage. (AO3a) Some evaluative comment on whether the regulatory framework is effective. (AO3b)

Demonstrates comprehensive application — thoroughly evaluates each specific failure against the relevant UK GDPR obligation, the severity of consequences, the full impact on individuals (financial harm, right to compensation), and the implications for DataVault as an organisation. Analyses the effectiveness of UK GDPR as a regulatory framework. (AO2) Demonstrates thorough analysis — critically evaluates the interplay between technical, procedural, and structural failures; examines how the ICO enforcement mechanism functions; and considers the systemic lessons from the breach. (AO3a) Reaches a well-reasoned, evidence-based conclusion about DataVault's compliance failures and the overall effectiveness of UK GDPR in protecting individuals, with acknowledgement of both the strengths and limitations of the regulatory framework. (AO3b)

scenario: Tidewater Supermarket uses facial recognition cameras at its entrances to identify returning customers and personalise their shopping experience. The facial data is stored on the supermarket's servers.

topic: F2.1.5 Data protection legislation — subject access rights
scenario: Crestfield Bank holds personal and financial data on all its account holders. A customer submits a Subject Access Request (SAR) asking for all data held about them.
question: Describe the process the bank must follow to respond to the Subject Access Request in accordance with UK GDPR.

points: The bank must acknowledge the request and respond within one calendar month (1)
The bank must verify the identity of the requester before releasing any data (1)

topic: F1.1.1 Privacy / F1.1.3 Unequal access / F2.1.5 Data protection / F1.1.6 Acceptable use policies
scenario: Oakvale Council is planning to replace all its public-facing services with a single digital platform. Residents will be able to apply for housing benefit, report environmental issues, and pay council tax online. Paper and telephone options will be removed. The council will collect and store extensive personal data including financial information, health details for benefit applications, and addresses.
question: Discuss the implications of Oakvale Council's move to a digital-only platform for residents and the council's legal obligations regarding the personal data collected.

indicative_content: Benefits: efficiency, cost saving, 24/7 access for residents with internet, faster processing of applications
Digital-only excludes residents without internet access or digital skills — elderly, low-income, rural
Removing telephone/paper options raises serious fairness concerns for those without IT access
Legal challenge under Equality Act 2010 if digital-only indirectly discriminates against protected groups
UK GDPR applies to all personal data collected — council must have lawful bases for processing
Financial and health data are sensitive and require appropriate security measures
Council must provide a clear privacy notice and inform residents how their data will be used
Residents have rights to access, correct, and delete their data under UK GDPR
A data breach involving housing benefit or health data would have serious consequences
The council must balance modernisation and efficiency against its duty of care to all residents
